steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The United States has used remotely piloted Unmanned Aircraft Vehicles (UAV) in its military services for several decades. Military analysts have pointed out that UAVs are attractive both strategically and tactically, since they are cheaper to deploy than crewed (manned) aircraft and they can do dangerous missions without risking human lives.

Also, more and more sophisticated UAVs are being introduced, supported by advances in machine learning (ML), and so several new types of missions are now within reach. These include cargo and resupply, air-to-air combat, close air support, communication relays, aerial refueling, search-and-rescue, and counter-terrorism missions. Because of the increased technological sophistication and the reduced size, it is becoming clear that UAVs are well-suited to many types of missions that until very recently only crewed aircraft could perform successfully. This could let the military station UAVs closer to the front lines than crewed aircraft, which could reduce the time it takes to carry out time-sensitive missions.

As the US withdraws from conflicts around the world, the military will have to rely more and more on UAVs for various missions, including intelligence, surveillance, and acquisition of ground targets in counter-terrorism missions.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The United States has used remotely piloted Unmanned Aircraft Vehicles (UAV) in its military services for several decades. Military analysts have pointed out that UAVs are attractive both strategically and tactically, since they are cheaper to deploy than crewed (manned) aircraft and they can do dangerous missions without risking human lives.

Also, more and more sophisticated UAVs are being introduced, supported by advances in machine learning (ML), and so several new types of missions are now within reach. These include cargo and resupply, air-to-air combat, close air support, communication relays, aerial refueling, search-and-rescue, and counter-terrorism missions. Because of the increased technological sophistication and the reduced size, it is becoming clear that UAVs are well-suited to many types of missions that until very recently only crewed aircraft could perform successfully. This could let the military station UAVs closer to the front lines than crewed aircraft, which could reduce the time it takes to carry out time-sensitive missions.

As the US withdraws from conflicts around the world, the military will have to rely more and more on UAVs for various missions, including intelligence, surveillance, and acquisition of ground targets in counter-terrorism missions.

The U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) is developing several experimental concepts that explore new ways of using future generation UAVs, such as aircraft system-of-systems, swarming, and lethal autonomous weapons. In line with this effort, the main vision of this paper is to take UAVs to the next level of sophistication, by enabling autonomous UAVs to carry out strike missions against entrenched high-value terrorists.

In the past these missions were done by Special Operations personnel and/or by remotely-piloted UAVs. But recent advances in blockchain technologies, smart contracts, and ML have made it possible for autonomous UAVs to carry out these missions successfully. Our first main contribution is to identify the main challenges that have to be overcome to implement our vision. Our second main contribution is to propose preliminary solutions to these challenges. As far as we know, this is the first paper in the open literature available to us that discusses the challenges in making such missions feasible and how these challenges can be overcome.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section II reviews related work. Section III gives the background information that is needed. Section IV introduces our working scenario and basic assumptions. Section V identifies some of the main challenges in enabling autonomous strike UAVs. Section VI gives preliminary solutions to the challenges from Section V. In Section VII, given a collection of tasks T_{1},\ T_{2},\ \cdots,\ T_{n} that have to be executed as part of the mission, we evaluate the conditional probability that a future task, say T_{i+1}, is completed successfully, given the completion status of the task that is currently executed, T_{i}. Section VIII identifies some of the sensors provided in the UAV to support its autonomous mission. Section IX gives the details of our ML framework for autonomous strike UAVs and a number of empirical evaluations. Section X discusses advanced ML techniques and how they are relevant to our research. Section XI gives concluding remarks and directions for future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
For several decades, the United States has employed remotely piloted Unmanned Aircraft Vehicles (UAV) across its military services [1]. As several military analysts have pointed out, UAVs are attractive from both strategic and tactical standpoints, because they are cheaper to deploy than crewed (i.e., manned) aircraft and can carry out dangerous missions without risking human lives [2].

In addition, with the gradual introduction of more sophisticated UAVs, supported by advances in machine learning (ML), several new types of missions are now within reach. These include cargo and resupply, air-to-air combat, close air support, communication relays, aerial refueling, search-and-rescue, and counter-terrorism missions [3]. It is becoming evident that, due to increased technological sophistication and reduced size, UAVs are well-suited to many types of missions that, until very recently, could only be performed successfully by crewed aircraft. This could enable the military to station UAVs closer to the front lines than crewed aircraft, potentially reducing the time needed to carry out time-sensitive missions.

As the US withdraws from conflicts around the world, the military will have to rely increasingly on UAVs for various missions, including intelligence, surveillance, and acquisition of ground targets in counter-terrorism missions [4,5].

It is widely known that the U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) is developing several experimental concepts, such as aircraft system-of-systems, swarming, and lethal autonomous weapons, that explore new ways of employing future generation UAVs [6,7,8,3]. Aligned with this effort, the main vision of this paper is to take UAVs to the next level of sophistication by enabling autonomous UAVs to carry out strike missions against entrenched high-value terrorists.

While in the past such missions were carried out by Special Operations personnel and/or by remotely-piloted UAVs, recent advances in blockchain technologies, smart contracts, and ML have made it possible for autonomous UAVs to carry them out successfully. Our first main contribution is to identify the main challenges that must be overcome to implement our vision; our second main contribution is to propose preliminary solutions to those challenges. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first paper in the open literature available to us that discusses the challenges inherent in making such missions feasible and the ways in which these challenges can be overcome.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews related work. Section III then provides the necessary background information. Section IV introduces our working scenario and basic assumptions. Section V identifies some of the main challenges involved in enabling autonomous strike UAVs. Next, Section VI provides preliminary solutions to the challenges identified in Section V. Section VII, given a collection of tasks T_{1},\ T_{2},\ \cdots,\ T_{n} that have to be executed as part of the mission, evaluates the conditional probability of a successful completion of a future task, say T_{i+1}, given the completion status of the currently executed task, T_{i}. Section VIII identifies some of the sensors provided in the UAV in support of its autonomous mission. Section IX offers the details of our ML framework in support of autonomous strike UAVs, along with a host of empirical evaluations. Section X discusses advanced ML techniques and their relevance to our research. Finally, Section XI offers concluding remarks and maps out directions for future work.
